summary:
Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime, and separately under a state legal environment in which courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans legislation under the Montana Constitution. In the July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment, Montana is the only state to improve its ranking; laws that would ordinarily place it among the worst states have not taken full effect because of that court record. Adult restrictions that were passed remain unenforced pending litigation, while federal policy shifts and litigation keep the youth-side picture unstable.

On 24 March 2026 Montana enacted Senate Bill 437, defining sex as a binary of male or female based on primary sexual anatomy and reproductive system (female defined as ova-based, male as sperm-based), and defining man, woman, mother and father on that basis. The statute provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role. The definitions apply across more than 60 sections of state law, including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, and applicants for driver's and marriage licences must list sex as so defined. Plaintiffs sought in April 2026 to add SB 437 to ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to Senate Bill 458, which was struck down in February 2025 by District Judge Leslie Halligan for violating the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution.

Identity-document changes remain contested. On 9 September 2022 Montana prohibited changing sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test; a court order blocked that rule on 15 September 2022 and the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied. A February 2023 bill prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents was signed on 19 May 2023 and blocked by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan. After an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, upheld 15 April 2026 by the Montana Supreme Court, which held that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. The December 2024 Helena district court order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule barring gender-identity-based changes to birth-certificate sex and the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate to change driver's-licence sex.

Facilities rules have been repeatedly restrained. In February 2025 the legislature passed HB 121 requiring bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; the ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta temporarily restrained the law, finding it motivated by animus and unsupported by evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A 2018 Montana Family Foundation initiative to require public bathroom use corresponding to birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures, and on 3 December 2024 the Montana House voted down a proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with gender.

Gender-affirming care for trans minors was prohibited by SB 99, signed 28 April 2023 and described as the most comprehensive such prohibition in the United States. District Judge Jason Marks preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender constitutes sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest; the Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class. Judge Marks permanently struck the law down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly.

A 2021 law banning transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Greg Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Montana hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed religious-belief legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people. In May 2023 HB 359 prohibited sexually oriented or obscene performances in public spaces where minors may be present and explicitly barred drag story hours at publicly funded schools and libraries, leading a Butte-Silver Bow library to cancel a transgender woman's reading; District Judge Brian Morris issued a temporary restraining order in July 2023, extended October 2024, blocking enforcement as vague and overbroad with risk of disproportionate enforcement against trans, Two-Spirit and gender-nonconforming people. A March 2025 bill, HB 675, defining drag as inherently sexual was defeated with 13 Republicans joining Democrats.

Discrimination protections exist at state-executive and local level. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules by Governor Marc Racicot, broadened by Executive Order 41-2008 in November 2008 under Governor Brian Schweitzer, and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016 by Governor Steve Bullock. Federal Title VII protections for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County apply in Montana. Ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations; Missoula County's ordinance covers county employees only.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined enforcement of the state ban, later mooted by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015; the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019. Montana permits adoption with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, with Kulstad v. Maniaci affirmed 6-1 on 7 October 2009. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997.

On 6 March 2025 House Bill 819 was debated and signed by Governor Gianforte in May 2025 with immediate effect, prohibiting flags representing political party, race, sexual orientation, gender or political ideology on government property and public schools, thereby banning Pride and other LGBTQ flags while permitting specified historical and official flags. Missoula adopted a rainbow pride flag as its municipal flag, effectively exempting it statewide.
tangentialFactors:
Montana's trajectory diverges from the national pattern: it is the only state to improve in the 2026 rankings, because state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans laws under the state constitution. Adult restrictions passed by the legislature have not taken full effect as a result.

The youth-side picture remains unstable both in Montana and nationally, driven by federal policy shifts and ongoing litigation over gender-affirming care and school-related rules.

The gap between statutes on the books and enforceable law is wide in Montana. SB 458 (2023) was struck down in February 2025, SB 99's care ban was permanently struck down in May 2025, the 2021 sports ban was struck down in September 2022, HB 121's facilities segregation was restrained in April 2025, and the 2022 and 2023 document-change restrictions were preliminarily enjoined in December 2024 and upheld by the Montana Supreme Court in April 2026. SB 437, enacted 24 March 2026, is the live legislative front and is being challenged as identical to the struck-down SB 458.

Montana's hate-crime statutes omit gender identity, so prosecution of such offences falls to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.
localsOnly:
Montana residents can change gender markers on identity documents under rules that have shifted repeatedly: surgery requirements were removed in December 2017 in favour of a Correction Affidavit, Gender Designation Form, court order and doctor letter for licences; an April 2021 law reintroducing surgical procedures and a court order was blocked in April 2022 for lack of clear legal definitions; the Department then imposed a temporary emergency rule in May 2022 banning updates, made permanent months later. Enforcement of that regime is currently paused by the December 2024 preliminary injunction, upheld by the Montana Supreme Court on 15 April 2026.

State employment and state-contractor discrimination on the basis of gender identity is barred by executive order, and local ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish extend protection to private employment, housing and public accommodations. Missoula County's ordinance covers county employees only.

HB 819, effective May 2025, bars government properties and public schools from flying flags representing sexual orientation or gender, which has been read to prohibit Pride flags; Missoula's adoption of a rainbow flag as its municipal flag operates as an exemption. A May 2021 parental opt-in law requires parental consent before K-12 sex education.

Montana permits adoption with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised if married, and surrogacy is unregulated with courts generally favourable to pre-birth parentage orders.
